subtopics.name: Gibbs Free Energy Change & Gibbs Equation

parts.problem_md:
Carbon dioxide and hydrogen can react to form methanol.

CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>OH (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

Data for standard enthalpy of formation and standard entropy is shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

|   | CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | H<sub>2</sub> (g) | CH<sub>3</sub>OH (g) | H<sub>2</sub>O (g) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | -394 | 0 | -201 | -242 |
| *S*<sup>θ</sup> / J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> | 214 | 131 | 238 | 189 |

i) Calculate the standard enthalpy change, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction. Show your working.

[2]

ii) Calculate the standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction. Show your working.

[2]

iii) Hence, calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction at 790 K. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the standard thermodynamic quantities for the reaction:

i) Standard enthalpy change, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>:

- Apply Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>(products) − ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>(reactants) and substitute values:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = [(−201) + (−242)] − [(−394) + (3 x 0)]

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −443 − (−394) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = **−49 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution into the Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> expression
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −49 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow −48 to −50 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

ii) Standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

- Apply Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants) and substitute values:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [(238) + (189)] − [(214) + (3 x 131)]

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 427 − 607 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **−180 J K**<sup>**-1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with 3 x 131 for H<sub>2</sub> (g)
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = −180 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow −179 to −181 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

iii) Standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, at 790 K:

- Convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> and substitute into Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −49 − (790 x (−0.180))

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −49 + 142.2 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = **+93.2 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> converted to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = +93.2 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>; allow error carried forward from (i) and (ii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> In part (iii), before substituting into Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> by dividing by 1000:
> 
> −180 / 1000 = −0.180 kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> In part (ii), remember to multiply *S*<sup>θ</sup>(H<sub>2</sub>, g) by 3 (its stoichiometric coefficient) before summing.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Carbon dioxide and hydrogen can react to form methanol.

CO₂ (g) + 3H₂ (g) ⇌ CH₃OH (g) + H₂O (g)

iii) Hence, calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*^θ^, for this reaction at 790 K. Show your working.

iii) Standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*^θ^, at 790 K:

Δ*G*^θ^ = +93.2 kJ mol^-1^

Use your answer to part **(a)(iii)** to state whether this reaction is feasible at 790 K.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Using the answer to (a)(iii) to state whether the reaction is feasible at 790 K:
> 
> - The reaction is not feasible at 790 K / Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is positive **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A reaction is feasible when Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> < 0. Since Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = +93.2 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> at 790 K, the reaction is not feasible at this temperature.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Carbon dioxide and hydrogen can react to form methanol.

CO₂ (g) + 3H₂ (g) ⇌ CH₃OH (g) + H₂O (g)

Data for standard enthalpy of formation and standard entropy is shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

|   | CO₂ (g) | H₂ (g) | CH₃OH (g) | H₂O (g) |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| ΔH°f / kJ mol⁻¹ | -394 | 0 | -201 | -242 |
| S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ | 214 | 131 | 238 | 189 |

i) Calculate the standard enthalpy change, ΔH°, for this reaction. Show your working.

ii) Calculate the standard entropy change, ΔS°, for this reaction. Show your working.

Using your answers to parts **(a)(i)** and **(a)(ii)**, calculate the temperature below which this reaction is feasible. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the temperature below which the reaction is feasible:

- At the feasibility boundary, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0, so *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

*T* = −49 / −0.180 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate *T*:

*T* = **272 K** **[1 mark]**

The reaction is feasible when *T* < 272 K

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> with Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> in kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *T* = 272 K; allow 270 to 275 K
> 
> Allow error carried forward from (a)(i) and (a)(ii)
> 
> The feasibility statement (*T* < 272 K) is not required for marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> At the feasibility boundary, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0:
> 
> 0 = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> Remember to convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> (−0.180) before dividing, to match the units of Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Carbon dioxide and hydrogen can react to form methanol.

CO₂ (g) + 3H₂ (g) ⇌ CH₃OH (g) + H₂O (g)

Explain why the reaction in part **(a)** has a negative entropy change.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Why the reaction in part (a) has a negative entropy change:
> 
> - Fewer moles / molecules of gas are produced than are consumed in the reaction **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In the equation CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>OH (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (g), there are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 moles of gas on the right. Fewer moles of gas means less disorder, so entropy decreases (Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> < 0).

parts.problem_md:
Using Table 4.1, calculate the entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for the combustion of ethanol at 298 K. Show your working.

**Table 4.1**

| **substance** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH (l) | O<sub>2</sub> (g) | CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | H<sub>2</sub>O (g) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ***S***<sup>**θ**</sup>** / J K**<sup>-1</sup>** mol**<sup>-1</sup> | +161 | +205.2 | +213.8 | +188.8 |

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = ........................... (J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>)
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for the combustion of ethanol at 298 K:

- Write the expression and substitute values:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants)

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [(2 x 213.8) + (3 x 188.8)] − [(1 x 161) + (3 x 205.2)] **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 994 − 776.6

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **+217.4 J K**<sup>**-1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow 217 to 218 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward if the expression is set up correctly but arithmetic is incorrect

> **[exam-tip]**
> Multiply each *S*<sup>θ</sup> value by its stoichiometric coefficient before summing:
> 
> - 2 x *S*<sup>θ</sup> CO<sub>2</sub> (g)
> - 3 x *S*<sup>θ</sup> H<sub>2</sub>O (g)
> - 3 x *S*<sup>θ</sup> O<sub>2</sub> (g)
> 
> Forgetting to apply stoichiometric coefficients is a common error in this type of calculation.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Using Table 4.1, calculate the entropy change, Δ*S*^θ^, for the combustion of ethanol at 298 K. Show your working.

**Table 4.1**

| **substance** | CH~3~CH~2~OH (l) | O~2~ (g) | CO~2~ (g) | H~2~O (g) |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| ***S***^**θ**^** / J K**^-1^** mol**^-1^ | +161 | +205.2 | +213.8 | +188.8 |

Using the value of Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> given in part **(a)** and your answer to part **(a)**, calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, for the combustion of ethanol at 298 K. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, for the combustion of ethanol at 298 K:

- Write the expression:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> and substitute values:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 217.4 / 1000 = 0.2174 kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −1367 − (298 x 0.2174)

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −1367 − 64.8 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = **−1432 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct expression Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> converted to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct final answer
> 
> Allow −1431 to −1433 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward from part (a)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Before substituting, convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> by dividing by 1000. This ensures the units match Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> (kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>):
> 
> 217.4 / 1000 = 0.2174 kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Alternatively, convert Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> from kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> to J mol<sup>-1</sup> by multiplying by 1000. Either method is valid, but avoid mixing units in the same calculation.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Using Table 4.1, calculate the entropy change, Δ*S*^θ^, for the combustion of ethanol at 298 K.

Δ*S*^θ^ = +217.4 J K^-1^ mol^-1^

Δ*H*^θ^ = −1367 kJ mol^-1^

Explain whether changing the temperature for the combustion of ethanol will affect the feasibility of the reaction.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Whether changing the temperature affects the feasibility of the combustion of ethanol:
> 
> - Changing the temperature does not affect the feasibility of the reaction **[1 mark]**
> - Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> is always negative
> **AND**
> Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is always positive **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is always negative at any temperature / the reaction is always feasible **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The feasibility of a reaction depends on the sign of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:
> 
> | Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> | Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> | Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> | Feasible? |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Negative (exothermic) | Positive (more disorder) | Always negative | At all temperatures |
> 
> When Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> < 0 and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> > 0, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is negative at all temperatures, so the reaction is always feasible regardless of temperature.

parts.problem_md:
Free energy changes can be used to predict the feasibility of chemical reactions and processes.

Table 3.1 shows the equations of five different chemical reactions or processes.

Complete the table to show the sign of Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for each chemical reaction and process.

**Table 3.1**

| **chemical reaction or process** | **sign of Δ*****S***<sup>**θ**</sup> |
|---|---|
| MgCl<sub>2</sub> (s) + (aq) → MgCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) |   |
| Ca (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → CaSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) |   |
| Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (s) + 10H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>•10H<sub>2</sub>O (s) |   |
| 2CO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g) |   |
| C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (g) → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (l) |   |
parts.solution_md:
The completed table is:

| **chemical reaction or process** | **sign of Δ*****S***<sup>**θ**</sup> |
|---|---|
| MgCl<sub>2</sub> (s) + (aq) → MgCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) | **Final answer:** **+** |
| Ca (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → CaSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) | **Final answer:** **+** |
| Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (s) + 10H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>•10H<sub>2</sub>O (s) | **Final answer:** **−** |
| 2CO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | **Final answer:** **−** |
| C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (g) → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (l) | **Final answer:** **−** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 2 marks for all 5 signs correct
> 
> 1 mark for 3 or 4 signs correct
> 
> 0 marks for 2 or fewer signs correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> Entropy increases (Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> positive) when the system becomes more disordered; it decreases (Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> negative) when the system becomes more ordered. Use state symbols as a guide:
> 
> - Solid or liquid → gas: entropy increases (+)
> - Gas → liquid or solid: entropy decreases (−)
> - Fewer moles of gas in products than reactants: entropy decreases (−)
> - More moles of gas in products: entropy increases (+)
> - Dissolving an ionic solid: entropy increases (+)
> 
> For the hydrated salt Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>•10H<sub>2</sub>O: a solid and a liquid combine to form a solid, so disorder decreases (−).

parts.problem_md:
The enthalpy and entropy changes of a reaction are both negative.

Explain how the feasibility of this reaction will change as the temperature decreases.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> How feasibility changes as temperature decreases when both Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> are negative:
> 
> - As temperature decreases, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> decreases
> **AND**
> the reaction becomes more feasible **[1 mark]**
> - Because *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> decreases in magnitude / becomes less negative **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> are both negative, the feasibility depends on temperature:
> 
> | Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> | Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> | Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> | Feasible? |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Negative | Negative | Negative at low *T* | At low temperatures |
> 
> To see this numerically, substitute imaginary values. For example, with Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −100 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = −0.10 kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>:
> 
> - At *T* = 100 K: Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −100 − (100 x −0.10) = −90 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (feasible)
> - At *T* = 1500 K: Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −100 − (1500 x −0.10) = +50 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (not feasible)
> 
> As *T* increases, −*T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> becomes more positive, pushing Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> positive. The reaction is feasible only at low temperatures.

parts.problem_md:
The equation for this reversible reaction is:

2SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2SO<sub>3</sub> (g)

Use the information in Table 3.2 to answer the following.

**Table 3.2**

|   | SO<sub>2</sub> | O<sub>2</sub> | SO<sub>3</sub> |
|---|---|---|---|
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | −296.8 | 0 | −395.7 |
| *S*<sup>θ</sup> / J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> | 248.2 | 205.1 | 256.8 |

i) Calculate the standard enthalpy change, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, for the reaction. Show your working.

[2]

ii) Calculate the standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for the reaction. Show your working.

[2]

iii) Calculate the temperature below which this reaction is feasible. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
To calculate thermodynamic quantities for the reaction between SO<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>:

i) Standard enthalpy change, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>:

- Apply Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>(products) − ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>(reactants) and substitute values:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = [2 x (−395.7)] − [2 x (−296.8) + 0]

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −791.4 − (−593.6) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = **−197.8 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with 2 x (−395.7) and 2 x (−296.8)
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −197.8 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow −197 to −198 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

ii) Standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

- Apply Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants) and substitute values:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [2 x 256.8] − [2 x 248.2 + 205.1]

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 513.6 − 701.5 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **−187.9 J K**<sup>**-1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with 2 x 256.8, 2 x 248.2, and 205.1
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = −187.9 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow −187 to −189 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward from (c)(i)

iii) Temperature below which the reaction is feasible:

- At the feasibility boundary, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0; convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> and find *T*:

*T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>

*T* = −197.8 / −0.1879 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate *T*:

*T* = **1053 K** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) 1 mark for correct substitution *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> with Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> converted to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *T* = 1053 K
> 
> Allow 1050 to 1060 K
> 
> Allow error carried forward from (c)(i) and (c)(ii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Before calculating *T*, convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> by dividing by 1000:
> 
> −187.9 / 1000 = −0.1879 kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Since both Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> are negative, the two negatives cancel when dividing, giving a positive temperature value.
> 
> Note: Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> of O<sub>2</sub> is 0 (element in standard state), but *S*<sup>θ</sup> of O<sub>2</sub> is not 0, which means that it must be included in the Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> calculation.

parts.problem_md:
Ammonium chloride, NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, can dissociate to form ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, and hydrogen chloride, HCl.

NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (s) → NH<sub>3</sub> (g) + HCl (g)

Explain why the standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction is positive.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The standard entropy change is positive because:
> 
> - A gas is formed from a solid **[1 mark]**
> - Gases have greater disorder / more ways to arrange energy than solids **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Entropy is a measure of the number of ways energy can be distributed among the particles in a system. The more arrangements possible, the higher the entropy.
> 
> When NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (s) dissociates, all products are gases. Gases have far more possible arrangements of particles than solids, so entropy increases significantly and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is positive.

parts.problem_md:
At 298 K, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +176 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = +285 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>.

Calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction at 298 K. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction at 298 K:

- Convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 285 ÷ 1000 = 0.285 kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Substitute into Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = (+176) − (298 x 0.285) **[1 mark]**

- Substitute values with Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> in kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>:

*T* = 178 / 0.165 **[1 mark]**

*T* = **1079 K** **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

This question is about the feasibility of a reaction.

Calcium carbonate can be thermally decomposed to make calcium oxide.

CaCO₃ (s) → CaO (s) + CO₂ (g)    ΔH° = +178 kJ mol⁻¹

Table 2.1 shows the standard entropies of each substance.

Table 2.1

| Substance | CaCO₃ (s) | CaO (s) | CO₂ (g) |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ | 89 | 40 | 214 |

Explain how the conditions can be changed for the reaction in **(a)** to make the reaction feasible.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> How conditions can be changed for the reaction in (a) to make it feasible:
> 
> - Increase the temperature **[1 mark]**
> - So that *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> > Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> becomes negative **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Since Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> is positive (endothermic) and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is also positive, increasing *T* increases the *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> term. Above 1079 K, *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> > Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, making Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> negative and the reaction feasible.

parts.problem_md:
The evaporation of water is an endothermic reaction but also a **feasible** reaction.

Explain why.

Refer to the entropy change that occurs and the change in the arrangement of water molecules.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Why the endothermic evaporation of water is feasible:
> 
> - When water evaporates, molecules become more disordered / spread out; the entropy change is positive **[1 mark]**
> - At sufficiently high temperatures, *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> > Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, so Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> < 0 and the reaction is feasible **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Even though evaporation is endothermic (Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> > 0), the large positive entropy change (liquid → gas, molecules become much more disordered) means the *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> term can exceed Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> at high enough temperatures, giving Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> < 0 and a feasible process.

parts.problem_md:
The equation for the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to form gaseous water is:

H<sub>2</sub> (g) + ½O<sub>2</sub> (g) → H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

Use the information in Table 2.2 to answer the following.

**Table 2.2**

|   | *S*<sup>θ</sup> / J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> | Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|---|
| H<sub>2</sub> (g) | 131 | 0 |
| O<sub>2</sub> (g) | 205 | 0 |
| H<sub>2</sub>O (g) | 189 | −242 |

i) Calculate the standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction. Show your working.

[2]

ii) Calculate the temperature above which this reaction is not feasible. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
To calculate thermodynamic quantities for the formation of gaseous water:

i) Standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

- Apply Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants) and substitute values:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 189 − [131 + (½ x 205)]

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 189 − 233.5 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **−44.5 J K**<sup>**-1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution including ½ x 205 for O<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = −44.5 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>; allow −44 to −45 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

ii) Temperature above which the reaction is not feasible:

- At the feasibility boundary, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0; rearrange to find *T*:

*T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>

- Convert Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> to J mol<sup>-1</sup> and substitute:

*T* = (−242 x 1000) / (−44.5) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate *T*:

*T* = **5438 K** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution using *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> with consistent units
> 
> 1 mark for *T* = 5438 K; allow 5400 to 5500 K
> 
> Allow error carried forward from (d)(i)

> **[exam-tip]**
> When calculating Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, remember the stoichiometric coefficient for O<sub>2</sub> is ½ — multiply its *S*<sup>θ</sup> value by ½ before subtracting. This is a common source of error.
> 
> To calculate *T*, ensure units are consistent: either convert Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> from kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> to J mol<sup>-1</sup> (multiply by 1000) to match J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>, or convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> (divide by 1000).

ii) Calculate the temperature above which this reaction is not feasible.

Explain what would happen to the sample of gaseous water if it was heated to a higher temperature than that calculated in part **(d)(ii)**.
parts.solution_md:

> What would happen to gaseous water heated above the temperature in (d)(ii):
